Cannabis 101

Full-Spectrum CBD, Explained: What's In It and What to Watch For

Full-spectrum CBD keeps the plant's other compounds, including a little THC. Here's what's in it, what the entourage idea rests on, and what to know about drug tests and the law.

By the High Society teamPublished October 24, 20267 min read

07min readCannabis 101
In this article
  1. CBD basics, and where it comes from: hemp or marijuana
  2. Three types: full-spectrum, broad-spectrum and isolate
  3. What full-spectrum CBD products contain: cannabinoids, terpenes, flavonoids
  4. The entourage idea and its evidence
  5. Why people use full-spectrum CBD: survey data, not claims
  6. Things to know: trace THC, drug tests and legal status
  7. Hemp-derived CBD versus dispensary CBD in Michigan
  8. Reading a certificate of analysis before you choose
  9. Frequently asked questions

Key takeaways

  • Full-spectrum CBD keeps the plant's other cannabinoids, terpenes and flavonoids, plus trace THC; broad-spectrum strips out the THC, and isolate is CBD alone.
  • The entourage idea, that plant compounds work better together, isn't established: studies so far are simple and contradictory.
  • In a 2026 study, daily CBD oil with as little as 0.5 mg of THC per dose produced positive urine drug tests.
  • Congress has narrowed the federal hemp definition; as of October 2026 the change is set to take effect in late 2026, and further changes are possible.
  • The FDA has approved one CBD medicine, and over-the-counter CBD products haven't been evaluated for effectiveness.

What is full-spectrum CBD? It's a CBD extract that keeps most of what the cannabis plant made alongside CBD: other cannabinoids, terpenes, flavonoids and a small amount of THC. That trace of THC matters more than anything else on the label, because it affects drug tests and legal status. Here's how full-spectrum compares with broad-spectrum and isolate, what the entourage idea really rests on, and how to read a lab report before you choose a product.

CBD basics, and where it comes from: hemp or marijuana

CBD, short for cannabidiol, is a cannabinoid that doesn't produce a high; our explainer on whether CBD is psychoactive covers why. It comes from the same plant whether the label says hemp or marijuana. The difference is legal, and it comes down to THC.

Under federal law as it stands in October 2026, hemp products are cannabis with no more than 0.3% delta-9 THC. Michigan counts THCA too: cannabis above 0.3% THC, including THCA, is marijuana that only licensed marijuana businesses may sell, while cannabis at or below that line is industrial hemp. Our guide to hemp vs. marijuana explains the split.

One more piece of background: the FDA has approved exactly one CBD medicine, Epidiolex, in 2018, for seizures linked to a few rare, severe conditions. It hasn't approved any other CBD product, and over-the-counter CBD hasn't been evaluated for whether it works for any disease.

Three types: full-spectrum, broad-spectrum and isolate

TypeWhat's in itTHC
Full-spectrumCBD plus the plant's other cannabinoids, terpenes and flavonoidsTrace amounts, kept on purpose
Broad-spectrumCBD plus many other plant compoundsRemoved or reduced
IsolatePurified CBDNone intended

Labels don't always match what's inside. When the FDA tested CBD products, many didn't contain the amount of CBD they claimed, and the agency has looked into reports of contaminants, including THC. If THC matters to you, the lab report beats the front of the package. Our overview of CBD types compares the three side by side.

What full-spectrum CBD products contain: cannabinoids, terpenes, flavonoids

A typical full-spectrum product holds:

  • CBD, the main cannabinoid
  • Minor cannabinoids such as CBG, CBC and CBN, usually in small amounts
  • Trace THC, which in hemp products stays at or below the federal limit by weight
  • Terpenes, the aroma compounds that give cannabis its scent
  • Flavonoids, plant pigments also found in fruits and vegetables
  • A carrier, often an oil such as MCT oil in tinctures

Amounts vary from product to product and batch to batch, which is why the certificate of analysis matters. Two bottles with the same CBD number can differ in everything else they carry.

The entourage idea and its evidence

Full-spectrum products are often sold on the "entourage effect," a theory that a plant's compounds work better together than CBD alone. The term began in an early lab study about the body's own cannabinoid-like messengers and was later stretched to cover whole-plant cannabis products.

A 2023 scoping review sorted the research for and against it. Supporters say it explains why some people prefer full-spectrum products; critics call it a marketing term. The reviewers found the literature in its infancy, with simple study designs, contradictory findings and clinical evidence that rests mostly on anecdotes and real-world reports. They suggested describing any such effects with ordinary pharmacology terms, like synergy, instead.

In short, it's an idea worth testing, not settled science. Our explainer on the entourage effect goes deeper.

Why people use full-spectrum CBD: survey data, not claims

What people say they use CBD for isn't the same as what CBD does. In a 2019 Gallup telephone survey of 2,543 U.S. adults, 14% said they personally used CBD products. Among users, the most common reasons given were pain (40%), anxiety (20%), insomnia (11%) and arthritis (8%). Gallup asked about CBD products in general, not full-spectrum specifically.

Surveys like this measure popularity and expectations, not results. CBD isn't free of side effects, either: the FDA notes it can cause liver injury, change how other medicines work and cause drowsiness. Talk with a clinician before using CBD, especially if you take medications, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or manage a health condition. For a look at what researchers are studying, see our CBD research roundup.

Things to know: trace THC, drug tests and legal status

Trace THC adds up. In a 2026 study, 60 healthy adults took CBD oil with 100 mg of CBD and 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 2.8 or 3.7 mg of THC per dose. During two weeks of twice-daily use, positive urine drug tests showed up in every group that received any THC. One sample from the CBD-only group tested positive, and two samples were still positive a week after people stopped. The authors noted that standard drug tests can't reliably tell legal hemp products from other cannabis.

Those THC doses didn't produce measurable differences in drug effects compared with CBD alone, which means you can fail a test without ever feeling high. If you're subject to drug testing, full-spectrum products are a real risk, and even THC-free products carry some.

Legal status is shifting too, as the next section explains.

Hemp-derived CBD versus dispensary CBD in Michigan

Michigan has two lanes for CBD:

  • Hemp-derived CBD: made from cannabis at or below 0.3% total THC, counting THCA. Michigan requires a state license to process or sell industrial hemp, and these products can be sold outside cannabis stores.
  • Dispensary CBD: CBD products made from marijuana, including ratio products that pair CBD with meaningful THC. Only licensed marijuana businesses may sell them, only adults 21 and older may buy them for adult use, and their labels name the testing lab and test date.

Federal law is shifting under the hemp lane. Congress has redefined hemp to count total THC, including THCA, and to exclude finished products with more than 0.4 mg per container of THC and similar cannabinoids. That change is set to take effect in late 2026, as of October 2026, and further changes are possible. Because full-spectrum products keep their natural THC, many could carry more than that per-container cap and fall outside the federal hemp definition once it fully applies.

Reading a certificate of analysis before you choose

A certificate of analysis, or COA, is the lab report for a product's batch. Before you choose, check:

  1. The lab and the date: an independent lab and a recent test.
  2. The batch number: it should match the number on your package.
  3. The cannabinoid panel: CBD, THC and THCA, plus any minor cannabinoids, listed as a percentage or in milligrams.
  4. Total THC per container: multiply the THC concentration by the product's weight. A 30-gram bottle at 0.2% THC holds about 60 mg of THC.
  5. Contaminant screens: results for pesticides, heavy metals, residual solvents and microbes.

Then match the product to your situation. If you're drug tested, full-spectrum isn't the right fit. If you're new to CBD, take a small first dose and give it time. And if you take any medication, check with your clinician first, since CBD can change how other drugs work.

Frequently asked questions

Can full-spectrum CBD make you feel high?

Usually not at hemp levels. In a 2026 study, adults who took 100 mg of CBD with up to 3.7 mg of THC showed no measurable difference in drug effects compared with CBD alone. Full-spectrum or ratio products with more THC, like those sold in licensed cannabis stores, are a different story and can be intoxicating, so check the THC figure on the label.

Could full-spectrum CBD cause a failed drug test?

Yes. In a 2026 study, people took CBD oil with as little as 0.5 mg of THC per dose, twice a day for two weeks. Positive urine tests appeared in every group that received any THC. Standard tests can't reliably tell hemp products from other cannabis. If you're tested, full-spectrum products are a real risk.

Can I buy full-spectrum CBD legally in Michigan?

Yes, within Michigan's rules. Hemp-derived CBD with no more than 0.3% total THC, counting THCA, is industrial hemp, and a state license is required to process or sell it. CBD products above that line are marijuana products that only licensed cannabis businesses may sell. Adult-use marijuana products are for adults 21 and older.

How is broad-spectrum different from full-spectrum?

Broad-spectrum keeps CBD and many of the plant's other compounds but has the THC removed or reduced. Full-spectrum keeps the THC too, in trace amounts for hemp products. Labels aren't always accurate, so if THC matters to you, check the lab report for THC and THCA rather than trusting the front of the package.

What changes for hemp CBD products in late 2026?

Federal law is narrowing the definition of hemp. The new definition counts total THC, including THCA, and excludes finished products with more than 0.4 mg per container of THC and similar cannabinoids. As of October 2026, it is set to take effect in late 2026; further changes are possible. Many full-spectrum products could fall outside the new definition.

  4. Wolinsky D et al. (2026), The acute and chronic pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of oral cannabidiol with and without low doses of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, Journal of Analytical Toxicologypmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  5. Public Law 119-37, Division B, sec. 781 (approved November 12, 2025): redefinition of hemp, 7 U.S.C. 1639ogovinfo.gov

21+

For adults 21 and older. Keep cannabis away from children and pets, and never drive after consuming. Michigan law does not allow cannabis use in public places.
